notes: 11 original AQA-style Year 1 Energetics questions, NOT official AQA past-paper items. Includes definitions, three calorimetry variants, Hess from formation/combustion/solutions, RP2 evaluation/graphs and gaseous mean bond enthalpies.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Explain the differences among exothermic, endothermic, activation energy, standard formation enthalpy and standard combustion enthalpy. State standard pressure and why the standard enthalpy of formation of O₂(g) is zero whereas that of O(g) is not. Write the standard formation equation for MgO(s).
markPoints: Exothermic reactions release heat to their surroundings and have negative ΔH; products are lower in enthalpy.
Endothermic reactions absorb heat and have positive ΔH; products are higher in enthalpy.
Activation energy is the energy barrier for a reaction and is not identical to ΔH.
Standard pressure is 100 kPa, at a stated temperature such as 298 K.
Standard formation enthalpy forms one mole of compound from elements in their standard states under standard conditions.
Standard combustion enthalpy relates to completely burning one mole of substance in oxygen under standard conditions.
Formation enthalpy of O₂(g) is zero in oxygen's standard elemental state; O(g) is not its standard state.
Mg(s)+½O₂(g)→MgO(s) is a valid one-mole formation equation.
questions.modelAnswer: Exothermic reactions release heat to their surroundings and have negative ΔH; products are lower in enthalpy. Endothermic reactions absorb heat and have positive ΔH; products are higher in enthalpy. Activation energy is the energy barrier for a reaction and is not identical to ΔH. Standard pressure is 100 kPa, at a stated temperature such as 298 K. Standard formation enthalpy forms one mole of compound from elements in their standard states under standard conditions. Standard combustion enthalpy relates to completely burning one mole of substance in oxygen under standard conditions. Formation enthalpy of O₂(g) is zero in oxygen's standard elemental state; O(g) is not its standard state. Mg(s)+½O₂(g)→MgO(s) is a valid one-mole formation equation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: In an insulated calorimeter 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl is mixed with 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. The temperature rises by 6.8°C. Assuming density 1.00 g cm⁻³, c=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and no heat losses, calculate molar enthalpy of neutralisation with its sign. Explain what heats up and what releases heat.
markPoints: Total solution volume is 25.0+25.0=50.0 cm³.
Mass of solution is approximately 50.0 g using 1.00 g cm⁻³ density.
Convert to q_solution=1.4212 kJ.
Moles of HCl=1.00×0.0250=0.0250 mol and NaOH is also 0.0250 mol.
One-to-one neutralisation produces 0.0250 mol water.
ΔH_reaction=−1.4212/0.0250=−56.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
Solution gains heat while the exothermic chemical reaction loses that heat.
questions.modelAnswer: Total solution volume is 25.0+25.0=50.0 cm³. Mass of solution is approximately 50.0 g using 1.00 g cm⁻³ density. q_solution=mcΔT=50.0×4.18×6.8=1421.2 J. Convert to q_solution=1.4212 kJ. Moles of HCl=1.00×0.0250=0.0250 mol and NaOH is also 0.0250 mol. One-to-one neutralisation produces 0.0250 mol water. ΔH_reaction=−1.4212/0.0250=−56.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Solution gains heat while the exothermic chemical reaction loses that heat.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: A 5.00 g sample of potassium chloride, Mr=74.6, dissolves in 100.0 g of water. The temperature falls from 22.0°C to 18.5°C. Assuming c=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for the water and negligible calorimeter heat capacity, estimate the molar enthalpy of solution and explain why the sign is positive.
markPoints: Temperature difference is ΔT=18.5−22.0=−3.5°C.
Mass used as directed is 100.0 g of water.
The solution reaction absorbs +1.463 kJ from the surroundings.
Estimated ΔH_solution=+1.463/0.0670≈+21.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
Positive enthalpy follows because dissolving is endothermic and the water cools.
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature difference is ΔT=18.5−22.0=−3.5°C. Mass used as directed is 100.0 g of water. q_water=100.0×4.18×(−3.5)=−1463 J. The solution reaction absorbs +1.463 kJ from the surroundings. Moles KCl=5.00/74.6≈0.0670 mol. Estimated ΔH_solution=+1.463/0.0670≈+21.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Positive enthalpy follows because dissolving is endothermic and the water cools.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: In a hypothetical fuel-calorimetry experiment, 0.600 g ethanol is consumed and the temperature of 100.0 g water rises by 12.0°C. Assume c_water=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and M(ethanol)=46.0 g mol⁻¹. Calculate the measured molar enthalpy of combustion and explain two reasons why it may be less exothermic than an accepted standard value.
markPoints: Heat absorbed by water q=100.0×4.18×12.0=5016 J.
Convert heat to 5.016 kJ.
Amount ethanol=0.600/46.0≈0.0130 mol.
Calculated ΔH=−5.016/(0.600/46.0)≈−385 kJ mol⁻¹.
The negative sign reflects heat release from the burning fuel.
Heat transfer to external surroundings or apparatus means less heat reaches the measured water.
Incomplete combustion may mean not all consumed ethanol follows the specified complete combustion equation.
questions.modelAnswer: Heat absorbed by water q=100.0×4.18×12.0=5016 J. Convert heat to 5.016 kJ. Amount ethanol=0.600/46.0≈0.0130 mol. Calculated ΔH=−5.016/(0.600/46.0)≈−385 kJ mol⁻¹. The negative sign reflects heat release from the burning fuel. Heat transfer to external surroundings or apparatus means less heat reaches the measured water. Incomplete combustion may mean not all consumed ethanol follows the specified complete combustion equation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: The reaction C₂H₄(g)+H₂(g)→C₂H₆(g) has standard formation enthalpies ΔfH° in kJ mol⁻¹: C₂H₄(g)=+52.3, H₂(g)=0, C₂H₆(g)=−84.7. Calculate the standard reaction enthalpy. Explain Hess's law and why the enthalpy value for elemental H₂(g) is zero.
markPoints: Hess's law says reaction enthalpy depends only on initial and final states, not route.
Use ΔH°reaction=ΣΔfH°(products)−ΣΔfH°(reactants).
Product sum is −84.7 kJ mol⁻¹ for C₂H₆(g).
Reactant sum is +52.3+0=+52.3 kJ mol⁻¹.
H₂(g) is elemental hydrogen in its standard state, so its ΔfH° is defined as zero.
questions.modelAnswer: Hess's law says reaction enthalpy depends only on initial and final states, not route. Use ΔH°reaction=ΣΔfH°(products)−ΣΔfH°(reactants). Product sum is −84.7 kJ mol⁻¹ for C₂H₆(g). Reactant sum is +52.3+0=+52.3 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH=−84.7−52.3=−137.0 kJ mol⁻¹. H₂(g) is elemental hydrogen in its standard state, so its ΔfH° is defined as zero.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Calculate ΔH° for hydrogenation C₂H₄(g)+H₂(g)→C₂H₆(g), using standard combustion enthalpies in kJ mol⁻¹: C₂H₄(g)=−1411, H₂(g)=−286 and C₂H₆(g)=−1560. Describe why the Hess combustion-cycle calculation subtracts products' combustion from reactants' combustion. All combustion products are CO₂(g) and H₂O(l).
markPoints: Both reactants and product may be fully combusted to the same final CO₂ and H₂O(l) state.
Apply Hess's law: ΔHreaction=ΣΔcH°reactants−ΣΔcH°products.
Total combustion enthalpy of reactants is −1411+(−286)=−1697 kJ mol⁻¹.
Combustion enthalpy of product C₂H₆ is −1560 kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔHreaction=−1697−(−1560)=−137 kJ mol⁻¹.
The product combustion pathway is reversed when reconstructing the target reaction, changing its sign.
questions.modelAnswer: Both reactants and product may be fully combusted to the same final CO₂ and H₂O(l) state. Apply Hess's law: ΔHreaction=ΣΔcH°reactants−ΣΔcH°products. Total combustion enthalpy of reactants is −1411+(−286)=−1697 kJ mol⁻¹. Combustion enthalpy of product C₂H₆ is −1560 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔHreaction=−1697−(−1560)=−137 kJ mol⁻¹. The product combustion pathway is reversed when reconstructing the target reaction, changing its sign.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: A student measures dissolution enthalpies for anhydrous CuSO₄(s) of −66 kJ mol⁻¹ and CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) of +12 kJ mol⁻¹. Both experiments finish in the same dilute aqueous CuSO₄ state. Use a labelled Hess relationship to calculate ΔH for CuSO₄(s)+5H₂O(l)→CuSO₄·5H₂O(s), explaining signs and why the same final aqueous state matters.
markPoints: The same dissolved final state allows the two routes to be compared by Hess's law.
Direct dissolution of anhydrous material has ΔH₁=−66 kJ mol⁻¹.
Dissolution of hydrated crystals has ΔH₂=+12 kJ mol⁻¹.
Path equation is ΔH₁=ΔHhydration+ΔH₂.
Thus ΔHhydration=ΔH₁−ΔH₂=−66−(+12).
Enthalpy of hydration reaction here is −78 kJ mol⁻¹, exothermic.
Identical final composition/states are needed for a valid Hess cycle.
questions.modelAnswer: The same dissolved final state allows the two routes to be compared by Hess's law. Direct dissolution of anhydrous material has ΔH₁=−66 kJ mol⁻¹. Dissolution of hydrated crystals has ΔH₂=+12 kJ mol⁻¹. Path equation is ΔH₁=ΔHhydration+ΔH₂. Thus ΔHhydration=ΔH₁−ΔH₂=−66−(+12). Enthalpy of hydration reaction here is −78 kJ mol⁻¹, exothermic. Identical final composition/states are needed for a valid Hess cycle.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Use the following mean gas-phase bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): C–H=413, O=O=498, C=O in CO₂=805 and O–H=463. Estimate ΔH for CH₄(g)+2O₂(g)→CO₂(g)+2H₂O(g). Show the bonds broken and formed and explain why this estimate differs from standard methane combustion to H₂O(l).
markPoints: Breaking four methane C–H bonds requires 4×413=1652 kJ mol⁻¹.
Breaking two O=O bonds requires 2×498=996 kJ mol⁻¹.
Total bonds broken energy=1652+996=2648 kJ mol⁻¹.
Two C=O bonds are formed in CO₂: energy 2×805=1610 kJ mol⁻¹.
Four O–H bonds are formed in two water molecules: energy 4×463=1852 kJ mol⁻¹.
Total bonds formed energy=1610+1852=3462 kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔH≈2648−3462=−814 kJ mol⁻¹ for formation of gaseous water.
Values are means from multiple gas molecules; standard combustion makes liquid water, requiring an additional phase enthalpy correction.
questions.modelAnswer: Breaking four methane C–H bonds requires 4×413=1652 kJ mol⁻¹. Breaking two O=O bonds requires 2×498=996 kJ mol⁻¹. Total bonds broken energy=1652+996=2648 kJ mol⁻¹. Two C=O bonds are formed in CO₂: energy 2×805=1610 kJ mol⁻¹. Four O–H bonds are formed in two water molecules: energy 4×463=1852 kJ mol⁻¹. Total bonds formed energy=1610+1852=3462 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH≈2648−3462=−814 kJ mol⁻¹ for formation of gaseous water. Values are means from multiple gas molecules; standard combustion makes liquid water, requiring an additional phase enthalpy correction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Define mean bond enthalpy and explain why energy is absorbed in bond breaking but released in bond formation. Explain why using tabulated average C–H bond enthalpies may produce a different calculated ΔH compared with experimental standard enthalpies of formation.
markPoints: Mean bond enthalpy is the mean energy to break one mole of a specific covalent bond in gaseous molecules.
Bond breaking requires energy input, so its term is positive.
Bond formation releases energy, so its contribution is negative.
Reaction estimate is the sum of bond energies broken minus the sum of bonds formed.
The C–H bond enthalpy varies with the rest of its molecule and its electronic environment.
Tabulated mean bond enthalpy is an average rather than the exact value for a specific bond.
Bond calculations generally assume gaseous species, whereas standard formation enthalpies include actual standard physical states.
questions.modelAnswer: Mean bond enthalpy is the mean energy to break one mole of a specific covalent bond in gaseous molecules. Bond breaking requires energy input, so its term is positive. Bond formation releases energy, so its contribution is negative. Reaction estimate is the sum of bond energies broken minus the sum of bonds formed. The C–H bond enthalpy varies with the rest of its molecule and its electronic environment. Tabulated mean bond enthalpy is an average rather than the exact value for a specific bond. Bond calculations generally assume gaseous species, whereas standard formation enthalpies include actual standard physical states.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Explain how a simple solution calorimetry experiment might underestimate the magnitude of an exothermic ΔH, how measurements and equipment cause uncertainty, and why a temperature–time graph can be extrapolated to the mixing time. Discuss the direction of error and how a more insulated calorimeter changes it.
markPoints: Heat loss to external surroundings reduces the measured solution temperature rise.
The smaller positive ΔT reduces q=mcΔT and makes the calculated exothermic ΔH less negative.
Some heat may also warm equipment not accounted for in the simple calculation.
Finite temperature measurement precision contributes uncertainty to ΔT.
Mass or volume measurement uncertainty contributes uncertainty to q or amount of reaction.
Extrapolating the cooling trend on a temperature-time plot back to the mixing instant helps estimate the temperature before heat was lost.
Better insulation reduces unintended heat exchange and usually improves the measured ΔH magnitude.
questions.modelAnswer: Heat loss to external surroundings reduces the measured solution temperature rise. The smaller positive ΔT reduces q=mcΔT and makes the calculated exothermic ΔH less negative. Some heat may also warm equipment not accounted for in the simple calculation. Finite temperature measurement precision contributes uncertainty to ΔT. Mass or volume measurement uncertainty contributes uncertainty to q or amount of reaction. Extrapolating the cooling trend on a temperature-time plot back to the mixing instant helps estimate the temperature before heat was lost. Better insulation reduces unintended heat exchange and usually improves the measured ΔH magnitude.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: A solution at 20.0°C reacts exothermically at t=60 s. After the reaction, recorded temperatures are: at t=120 s, 26.4°C; t=180 s, 25.8°C; t=240 s, 25.2°C. (a) Use a straight-line cooling trend to extrapolate temperature at t=60 s. (b) Find corrected ΔT. (c) Assuming 50.0 g solution, c=4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, and 0.0250 mol reacted, calculate corrected molar ΔH. Explain why direct use of 26.4°C would underestimate magnitude.
markPoints: Temperature falls by 0.6°C per 60 s in the post-reaction cooling line.
Extrapolate one minute backwards to t=60 s to estimate peak temperature 27.0°C.
Corrected temperature rise is 27.0−20.0=7.0°C.
q_solution=1.463 kJ and amount of reaction is 0.0250 mol.
Corrected ΔHreaction=−1.463/0.0250=−58.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
Using t=120 s gives ΔT=6.4°C and an apparently smaller heat output because cooling has already occurred.
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature falls by 0.6°C per 60 s in the post-reaction cooling line. Extrapolate one minute backwards to t=60 s to estimate peak temperature 27.0°C. Corrected temperature rise is 27.0−20.0=7.0°C. q_solution=50.0×4.18×7.0=1463 J. q_solution=1.463 kJ and amount of reaction is 0.0250 mol. Corrected ΔHreaction=−1.463/0.0250=−58.5 kJ mol⁻¹. Using t=120 s gives ΔT=6.4°C and an apparently smaller heat output because cooling has already occurred.
